To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a strong CTL and antibody responses are required to resolve HCV infection.
a weak CTL level can result in persistent HCV infection and evolution towards escape from antibody response, and this shift in balance of immune response can result in onset of liver disease.

(i) a strong CTL response can result either in clearance or in persistent infection, while a weak CTL response is associated with persistence; (ii) persistent infection is accompanied by ongoing antibody production and low levels of CTLs; (iii) evolution of the virus towards escape from antibodies results in shift of the balance of immune response towards pathology; (iv) the balance of the immune responses can be decisive for the clinical outcome
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of immune responses and viral evolution in determining the outcome of infection with hepatitis C virus.
the role of CTLs and antibodies in HCV dynamics and the role of immune responses in the evolution of the virus and the pathology of HCV infection.
the role of CTLs and antibodies in the dynamics and pathology of HCV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HCV infection can lead to persistent infection and liver pathology, but that the outcome is not predetermined and depends on the relative balance of antibody and CTL responses.
the CTLs are important in controlling HCV infection, and that the CTLs and antibodies can both play a role in HCV pathology.
the immune responses to HCV are not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune response is critical in determining the outcome of HCV infection.
the immune response can have a decisive impact on the course of infection and the development of pathology.
we are trying to understand the dynamics and pathology of HCV infection by using mathematical models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a weak CTL and antibody response may be sufficient to prevent clearance of the virus but may result in evolution towards antigenic escape.
the immune response is not simply an on/off phenomenon.
the balance of the immune responses is important for the outcome of infection.
